explanation:
The grid contains just two single pixels (an 8 and a 7) on a 0 background. In both demonstrations the output has every seed extended into a full horizontal line and a full vertical line of its own colour, spanning the whole grid — a "cross" through the seed. The only extra ingredient is colour 2: it appears exactly where a line of one seed crosses a line of the other seed. In pair 1 the 8 sits at (1,3) and the 7 at (7,6); the 8's row 1 meets the 7's column 6 at (1,6), and the 7's row 7 meets the 8's column 3 at (7,3) — those are precisely the two 2-cells in the output. Pair 2 has the same structure (seeds at (2,2) and (6,6), 2s at (2,6) and (6,2)). Each cross contributes 17 cells (9+9−1), minus one crossing with the other colour: 15 cells of each colour plus two 2s, matching the fact sheet counts exactly.

So the rule: for every non-background pixel, paint its whole row and whole column in its colour; any cell reached by lines of two different seeds becomes 2.

For the test input the seeds are 8 at (1,4) and 7 at (6,1). The 8 fills row 1 and column 4; the 7 fills row 6 and column 1; the crossings (1,1) and (6,4) become 2.
code:
def transform(grid):
    g = np.array(grid)
    bg = background(g)
    H, W = g.shape
    out = g.copy()
    seeds = [(y, x, int(g[y, x])) for y in range(H) for x in range(W) if g[y, x] != bg]

    # count how many seeds reach each cell via their row or column
    count = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=int)
    for (y, x, c) in seeds:
        out[y, :] = c
        out[:, x] = c
        reach = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool)
        reach[y, :] = True
        reach[:, x] = True
        count += reach.astype(int)
        emit(out, f"Extend the colour-{c} pixel at ({y},{x}) into a full row and full column of colour {c}")

    # cells where lines of different seeds cross become 2
    cross = count >= 2
    out[cross] = 2
    emit(out, "Mark every cell where lines of two different seeds cross with colour 2")
    return out
